clusters.name: execution_errors_no_finding
clusters.root_cause: The review pipeline terminated with an execution error before producing any finding object, so no severity, fix, or test was emitted. Because the failure is infrastructural rather than analytical, the same task_id (87ed5d93) recurs across three cases, indicating a single run that failed repeatedly or was retried without a successful completion. Likely contributors are tool invocation failures, malformed model output that failed schema validation, or budget exhaustion during the review loop.

clusters.name: accepted_security_finding_quality
clusters.root_cause: The SEC-EVAL finding was accepted and is a true positive, but the evidence is synthetic and the gate reports strong_evidence_count of 0 despite exact_location_evidence being true. The finding relies on a single local-rule scanner hit plus AST confirmation rather than independent corroboration, and the confidence of 0.85 sits just below a typical high-confidence threshold. This is not a false positive, but it shows the security path can pass a critical finding with weak corroboration, which risks both over-trust in synthetic cases and under-verification in real ones.

candidate_change.rationale: Cases 1-3 share one task_id and all failed with execution_error and null findings, so they cluster as a single pipeline failure rather than three independent analytical misses; the fix is to require an explicit execution_error finding instead of null. Case 4 is an accepted true-positive security finding, so it is not a false positive; its weakness is that a critical finding passed the gate with strong_evidence_count of 0 and confidence just under 0.9, which motivates the two-source corroboration rule and the critic delegation. The proposed changes are limited to prompt, delegation, tool-selection, and budget configuration and contain no production source-code edits.

finding.title: Arbitrary code execution via eval() on untrusted request input in parse_request
finding.explanation: The new function parse_request takes a request object and passes request["value"] directly into eval(). The diff context marks app.py as a network-boundary file, so request["value"] is attacker-controllable input arriving across a network trust boundary. There is no validation, normalization, allowlist, or sandboxing between the source (request["value"]) and the sensitive sink (eval). An attacker who can supply the request value can execute arbitrary Python expressions in the server process, leading to remote code execution, data disclosure, and full host compromise. The local-rule scanner independently flagged this call site as critical (SEC-EVAL) and the diff AST confirms a valid Call node at app.py line 2.
finding.fix: Remove eval() entirely. Replace it with an explicit parser or a strict allowlist/command map, e.g. parse the value with json.loads for structured data, or map an expected key to a fixed handler: HANDLERS = {"sum": lambda v: sum(v)}; return HANDLERS[request["value"]](...). If expression evaluation is genuinely required, use a restricted evaluator such as ast.literal_eval for literals only, and never pass raw request data to eval/exec.
finding.test: Add a regression test that calls parse_request with a malicious payload such as {"value": "__import__('os').system('id')"} and asserts it is rejected (raises/returns an error) and that no code executes, while a legitimate allowlisted input still returns the expected result.
